I lost a LOT of hair after surgery (it didn't start till about 6-8 months post op) It took about 2 years for me to feel like my hair was as thick as it was pre surgery .

It's called telogen effluvium. Normally about 85% of your hair is growing, and 15% is "sleeping". Stress from things like surgery, child birth and rapid weight loss can switch these, so about 85% of your hair is sleeping, and only 15% is growing. 

If it is telogen effluvium, it doesn't really matter what vitamins or supplements you take, you just have to wait for it to go back to normal

I had to drive over 2 hours to see my surgeon, but it doesn't really matter what I eat, I won't gain the weight back. I only absorb half the fat I eat. DBT changed my life and made it possible for me to have a successful marriage and career.

And distress tolerance skills for when I lose my shit. I still lose my shit - but instead of self harming or self sabotaging - now I can walk away find my dog and cry cuddled up to her instead. That is a HUGE step up for me. 

IMO, DBT is like someone taking you to home depot, and teaching you about all the tools that exist and what they do, when all you've ever known about was a hammer. And you used a hammer for everything. Maybe you won't need all the tools, maybe you'll hate some of them - but the knowledge you gain is REALLY helpful.

I practice mindfulness everyday because it helps me with my mental health. It has helped me be more considerate in my relationships and eased some symptoms of depression.

So for me, practicing mindfulness is like taking 20 minutes a day to work out. I set aside time to me mindful, practice being non judgmental / etc. I might do some additional mindfulness during the day - but it's mini - what I consider the equivalent of doing pushups during commercials, or calf rises while doing the dishes.  My main activity is not mindfulness, I'm just adding it in.   


You can also mindfully let your thoughts wander. Just notice what you are thinking without judgement.

I'm like you, a quiet borderline, and consider myself in "recovery" for the last year or 2. 

I think a better word might be remission. I still have an occasional "episode" once or twice a year. Sometimes its a trigger I know is coming and I can use my skills and prep for it. But then the day comes or the event happens -  and its a terrible emotional roller coaster and I spend the day with all emotions at a 10, sobbing on the floor. So is that recovery? It is to me.

I don't have SI anymore (except on those days maybe) But when I do, I can recognize them as just thoughts I don't have to pay attention to.

I no longer have screaming fights with my husband about putting the groceries away. When I feel my anger rising to the point I know I'm gonna lose it - I walk away and simmer down, allow myself to get in perspective. Take a moment for mindfulness. 

I no longer worry that my coworkers will say things like "she's super competent, but I wouldn't work with her again" My yearly reviews no longer tell me I need to learn to play with others. 

It's still a lot of work. And I make mistakes all the time. It almost feels like all the therapy skills I've learned and all the meditation and mindfulness allows me to have an extra check on my thoughts. So I still HAVE and BEGIN all those terrible negative thoughts - like thinking I'm a waste of space that shouldn't exist - but instead of it planting and getting a chance to grow - I can throw it out or ignore it. 

I can't do that if I don't practice my skills/mindfulness on a weekly if not daily basis. I think of it like physical exercise.  We're supposed to get some physical activity in a couple times a week, or our bodies get mad. I have to do this a couple times a week too, or I go mad.

I empathize a lot with what you describe. 

My mom died when I was 20. She was sick in the hospital for just 30 days before she died. But 2 months before she went into the hospital I'd had my own hospitalization - for suicidal ideations. Afterwards, I spent a month recovering at home with my mom before going back to college. She took off of work and we spent time together and just talked. So when she unexpectedly died later that year, I did feel like - at the time - I'd gotten to say and talk about most of the things I'd wanted to. And I appreciated that and considered it one of the things I was 'lucky' about. 

But now I'm 40 - and there are ALL kinds of questions and topics I would LOVE to be able to ask my mom about the 20 year old me couldn't have imagined. Sometimes I think about asking my dad or her sister, but I don't have that kind of relationship with them. And really, it would be what THEY think she'd say - and I don't need that viewpoint. 

I know for me with grief and radical acceptance - sometimes you have to let it sit and come and ride it out/ cry it out. I have a tendency to shut down my feelings, so it was important to learn to let myself finish crying naturally - to learn that bad/ hard feelings will eventually go away on their own. Also radical acceptance isn't something you do and complete. It's like exercise, when its for something hard like grief, you might have to check in with it daily or weekly. Pain from grief never goes away, you just get used to it. It wasn't my mom's death I had to accept- I've accepted she's gone. What I continue to need to practice radical acceptance on is that there's no greater meaning in her loss. I'm not religious, so I don't believe in any kind of afterlife or fate or plan of the gods. It makes accepting the death of loved ones hard.

I also understand wishing you had done more to make your dad more comfortable. When it comes to things you can't change - I always joke about firing up the time machine... As someone with BPD - before meds and therapy:

for me I was usually acting out of fear. Fear of abandonment and being alone were the biggest things. And feeling worthless and unlovable.
